A.explanation: A speed of $2 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ would give separation speed $0$, which is less than the $6 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ approach speed and so cannot be perfectly elastic.

B.explanation: A speed of $4 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ would give separation speed $2 \text{cm s}^{-1}$, which does not equal the $6 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ approach speed.

C.explanation: A speed of $6 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ would give separation speed $4 \text{cm s}^{-1}$, which is still less than the $6 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ approach speed.

D.explanation: A speed of $8 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ gives separation speed $8 - 2 = 6 \text{cm s}^{-1}$, equal to the approach speed as required for a perfectly elastic collision.

hints: Notice the given speeds along the line of impact: X approaches at $6 \text{cm s}^{-1}$, Y is stationary, and X continues forward at $2 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ after impact.
Recall what perfectly elastic means for relative motion: speed of approach of X and Y must equal speed of separation of Y and X.
Set the separation speed $v_Y - 2 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ equal to the approach speed $6 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ and solve for $v_Y$.
walkthrough: Identify the motion along the straight line: before collision $u_X = 6 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ and $u_Y = 0$, after collision $v_X = 2 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ in the same direction and $v_Y$ is unknown forward.
State the governing rule for a perfectly elastic collision in one dimension: speed of approach equals speed of separation.
Calculate speed of approach: $u_X - u_Y = 6 - 0 = 6 \text{cm s}^{-1}$.
Write speed of separation with Y now ahead of X: $v_Y - v_X = v_Y - 2 \text{cm s}^{-1}$.
Equate them: $v_Y - 2 = 6$, so $v_Y = 8 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ with correct unit $\text{cm s}^{-1}$.
This matches the $8 \text{cm s}^{-1}$ choice. This is option D.
